1. The project on one page

The problem. Lenders and auditors want to know early when a company is heading for a cash-flow crisis. The classic tools (Altman's Z-score, logit and hazard models) compare a firm with many other firms and need large samples of past failures. For mid-sized firms in India or the Gulf there are often no good peers and only a few years of history.

The idea. Instead of comparing a firm with others, compare it with its own past. Learn what 'normal' looks like for this one firm, then raise an alarm when its financial ratios drift persistently away from normal in the bad direction. The project builds this as a stack of layers, from simple ratio checks to statistical change detectors, and asks two questions: does a firm's own cash-flow history warn early? and when does cash flow hide the problem instead?

The two stories that motivated it. At Jyoti Structures (India, insolvency admitted 2017-07-04) operating cash flow turned negative in FY2014, 3.26 years before the event. At NMC Health (UAE/UK, administration 2020-04-09) reported cash flow looked healthy right up to the collapse; the trouble was hidden in the balance sheet (and, as it turned out, in debt that was never reported).

What we found, in five lines.

  1. The standard way of setting alarm thresholds is badly wrong with short histories. Thresholds meant to give 10% false alarms gave 34.2% on simulated healthy firms with 28 periods of history.
  2. It can be fixed cheaply. Three corrections bring the false-alarm rate to 8.4%, 7.2% and 8.4%; the best one costs only 1.6 points of detection.
  3. Watching several ratios beats watching cash alone when cash is quiet or massaged, but loses when the problem is in cash itself.
  4. The case studies match the two stories: cash warned early at Jyoti; at NMC only liquidity cover (cash ÷ short-term debt) warned, from FY2015.
  5. On 91 real US bankruptcies, simple pre-set rules beat everything else, and the statistical alarms barely beat chance (62.6% of failed firms flagged vs 54.3% of healthy ones). A post-hoc diagnosis explains why (Section 6).
Question (plain words)VerdictIn one line
H1Does Jyoti's own cash history warn ≥ 2 years early, using the statistical detector?INCONCLUSIVENot enough pre-crisis data to train the detector (needs BSE quarterly FY2010–13).
H2At NMC, did cash flags stay silent while balance-sheet flags fired?SUPPORTEDYes, but only one balance-sheet flag fired, so NMC is 'Other', not 'Masked', by our own rule.
H3Is watching many ratios better than one when cash is masked?SUPPORTEDYes in simulation: big win when cash is quiet or smoothed, clear loss when cash itself drifts.
H4Are standard alarm thresholds too trigger-happy with short histories?SUPPORTEDYes: several times more false alarms than promised, at every history length.
H5Can a cheap correction fix the thresholds?SUPPORTEDYes: all three fixes land within the tolerance; the parametric one costs least detection.

2. Key ideas in plain words

IdeaWhat it means here
Financial ratioA number that compares two items in the accounts, e.g. operating cash flow ÷ current liabilities. Ratios make firms of different size comparable and make a firm comparable with itself over time.
Orientation: lower = worseEvery ratio is flipped if needed so that a fall always means deterioration. Debtor days (how long customers take to pay) are bad when high, so the project uses minus debtor days (neg_dso). This lets one detector look for 'falls' in every ratio.
Operating cash flow (OCF)Cash actually generated by the business in a period, before investment and financing. Profits can be manipulated with accounting choices; cash is harder to fake. That is why the project is 'cash-first'.
Event and event timeThe event is the formal insolvency (court admission, administration, or a US bankruptcy 8-K filing). Event time counts years or quarters before it: τ = 0 is the period containing the event, τ = −1 the one before.
Rule flag (Layer 2)A simple pre-set test such as 'OCF below zero' or 'EBITDA covers interest less than 1.2 times'. Cheap, transparent, and fixed in advance.
Altman Z''-EMA classic distress score combining working capital, retained earnings, operating profit and equity, each scaled by assets. Below 4.35 is the 'distress zone'. Used as the benchmark everyone knows.
State-space / Kalman model (Layer 3)A model that keeps a running estimate of the 'normal level' of a ratio and predicts the next value. Its parameters are learned on the training years and then frozen. The standardised forecast error z = (actual − predicted) ÷ its usual size tells how surprising each new value is.
CUSUMA running total of bad surprises: St = max(0, St−1 − zt − k). Small surprises are absorbed by the allowance k = 0.5; a run of bad surprises makes S grow; an alarm sounds when S passes the threshold h. It catches slow, persistent drifts that no single quarter would reveal.
Multivariate CUSUM (Layer 4)The same idea on several ratios at once (Crosier's MCUSUM), using their joint covariance (estimated with Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage because the samples are small). It can notice that 'everything is a bit worse'. Its weakness: it reacts to change in any direction, including improvement.
False-alarm rate: nominal vs empiricalThe threshold h is chosen to promise, say, a 10% chance of a false alarm on a healthy firm over the monitored window (the nominal rate). The empirical rate is what actually happens when you run it on healthy firms. If empirical ≫ nominal, the thresholds are 'miscalibrated' (too trigger-happy).
Bootstrap and block bootstrap (Layer 5)To set h for one firm, we resample that firm's own past forecast errors many times (2,000 resamples), simulate the CUSUM on each fake future, and take the value exceeded only 10% of the time. 'Block' means we resample runs of consecutive quarters, not single ones, to keep their dependence.
Why short histories break itWith few years of data the model's parameters are guessed with error, and the handful of past errors under-represents how wild the future can be. Both make h too low, so alarms fire too often. Hypothesis H4 measures by how much.
The three fixes (H5)Inflation factor: multiply h by a factor that depends on history length, learned in simulation. Conformal threshold: set h directly from the CUSUM maxima of many similar healthy simulated firms. Parametric bootstrap with refitting: simulate new histories from the fitted model and re-estimate the model on each, so the threshold includes the estimation error.
Masking index (Layer 6)MI = (structural detector ÷ its threshold) − (cash detector ÷ its threshold). Positive means the balance-sheet side is alarming while cash looks calm: the crisis is 'masked'. The fingerprint records which detector fired first.
ArchetypesA pre-set rule labels each failed firm: Visible (OCF negative for two consecutive years or more), Masked (OCF positive throughout but at least two of three balance-sheet flags trip), or Other.
Pre-registrationAll hypotheses, rules and thresholds were written down, dated and fingerprinted (SHA-256 hash) before any detector was run. This prevents tuning the method until it 'works' on the known cases (hindsight bias).
Detection, false alarm, expected cost, AUCDetection = share of failed firms flagged before the event. False alarm = share of healthy matched firms flagged over the same window. Expected cost weighs a missed failure as several times worse than a false alarm. AUC = probability that a random failed firm looks worse than a random healthy one (0.5 = coin flip, 1 = perfect), a threshold-free measure.

3. The data

SourceWhatUsed forHow it was checked

SEC EDGAR (US)Quarterly XBRL filings: 150 firms with a bankruptcy 8-K (Item 1.03) in 2015–2023, 87 matched healthy controlsExternal test of Layers 0–6 on real dataIdentities per firm; first-filed values only (no hindsight restatements); controls never filed for bankruptcy; financials excluded
India cohort6 listed Indian firms admitted to insolvency 2017–2018 (RBI's 2017 large-defaulter lists), 5 size- and industry-matched healthy controls, Jet Airways as negative control; annual, Screener.inH6 (confirmatory test) and rule-level checksFrame and rule fingerprinted before any figure was read; parser reproduces Jyoti exactly; identities; controls never insolvent

Why the US panel? Layers 3–5 need at least 12 usable periods of history. NMC has 6 annual points and Jyoti none before FY14, and the cohort is annual too. EDGAR is free, machine-readable and large, so it is the place where the models can actually be fitted and tested on real companies. Of the 150 failed firms, 91 (and 46 of their controls) had enough clean quarterly history; the rest were dropped for documented reasons (too little history, identity failures, model failures) listed in edgar_funnel.csv. These rules were written into the config before the download.

Data decisions worth remembering
  • Accounting identities (assets = liabilities + equity, the profit bridge, the cash-conversion cycle) are checked before anything runs; a failure stops the run and names the firm, year and columns.
  • Missing years are never filled in. Section 7 shows why: interpolating Jyoti's FY2017 would invent a distress signal from a number that was never published.
  • Ratios with near-zero denominators are blanked (|denominator| ≤ 1% of total assets for sales-based ratios) instead of producing absurd values.
  • US quarterly data: year-to-date figures were turned into quarters, flows summed over the trailing twelve months, and only the first-filed value kept, so no later correction leaks back in time.

4. The method, layer by layer

Layer 0
Ratios and audit. Build oriented ratios, mask impossible values, check identities. Output: ratios_*.csv.
Layer 1
Event-time study. Line firms up by years/quarters before the event and plot each ratio against healthy controls.
Layer 2
Rule flags. Pre-set rules: OCF < 0; EBITDA/interest < 1.2; debtor days > 270; Altman Z''-EM < 4.35.
Layer 3
Cash detector. Kalman model on OCF ÷ current liabilities, standardised errors, one-sided CUSUM.
Layer 4
Multivariate detector. Kalman errors on cash plus structural ratios, Ledoit–Wolf covariance, Crosier MCUSUM.
Layer 5
Thresholds and alert tiers. Block-bootstrap thresholds (plus the corrections). Amber: either detector over its 10% threshold. Red: multivariate over its 5% threshold and a Layer 2 rule agrees.
Layer 6
Masking index and fingerprint. Which side (cash or structure) alarms, and which first; archetype rule.

Why layers? Each layer is useful on its own and cheaper than the next. A lender can stop at Layer 2 with very little data; Layers 3–5 need a longer history but adapt to each firm; Layer 6 says what kind of trouble it is. Running them side by side also lets the project test whether the expensive layers add anything over the cheap ones. Section 6 shows that on real US firms they mostly did not.

Training and monitoring. For each firm the history is split: a training window where the model learns 'normal', and a monitored window (16 quarters ending at the event on EDGAR) where alarms count. Nothing from the monitored window is used to fit the model or set the threshold. Healthy controls are monitored over exactly the same calendar window as their matched failed firm, so a control alarm is a real-world false alarm.

5. Results, hypothesis by hypothesis

Each hypothesis was written with explicit 'supported if' and 'refuted if' criteria before any detector ran (docs/PREREGISTRATION.md). The verdicts below are produced by code from those criteria, not chosen by hand.

H4: Are the standard thresholds too trigger-happy? SUPPORTED

Test. Simulate healthy firms (no deterioration at all), set each firm's threshold with the standard block bootstrap from its own training history, then count how many raise an alarm anyway.

History length n (periods)Promised 5% → actual (95% CI)Promised 10% → actual (95% CI)
1251.0% (46.6%–55.4%)54.0% (49.8%–58.4%)
1636.4% (32.2%–40.8%)39.4% (35.0%–43.8%)
2035.2% (31.0%–39.4%)39.8% (35.4%–44.0%)
2828.6% (24.6%–32.4%)34.2% (30.0%–38.4%)
4022.6% (19.0%–26.2%)27.4% (23.6%–31.2%)

Meaning. A lender told 'one in ten healthy firms will be flagged' would actually see about one in three at n = 28, and about one in two at n = 12. More history helps but never closes the gap within the range a real firm has. This is the project's most solid result: it is large, it holds at every n, and it shows up again on real US firms (Section 6).

H5: Can it be fixed cheaply? SUPPORTED

Test. Fit each correction on one set of simulated firms, then test it on a different set (held out). Pre-registered success: within ±3 points of the promised 10% at n = 28.

MethodFalse alarms, promised 10% (95% CI)False alarms, promised 5%Detection of a real drift (S1)Detection lost vs no correction
No correction (standard)34.2% (30.2%–38.2%)28.6%68.0%0.0 points
Inflation factor8.4% (6.0%–10.8%)6.4%43.6%24.4 points
Conformal threshold7.2% (5.0%–9.6%)4.6%65.6%2.4 points
Parametric bootstrap (refit)8.4% (6.2%–10.8%)4.8%66.4%1.6 points

Meaning. All three fixes work, but they are not equal. The inflation factor (h × 2.50 at n = 28) also raises the threshold of firms whose threshold was already fine, so it throws away 24.4 points of detection. The parametric bootstrap targets the actual source of the error (uncertain parameters) and loses almost nothing. The conformal threshold is nearly as good but needs a pool of similar healthy firms, which a single-firm monitor does not have.

H3: Many ratios or one? SUPPORTED

Test. Four simulated scenarios: S1 the cash ratio drifts down; S2 cash is fine but the other ratios deteriorate; S3 everything drifts a little; S4 everything deteriorates but reported cash is smoothed (concealment). All detectors are first tuned to the same 10% false-alarm rate, so the comparison is fair.

ScenarioARIMA + CUSUMKalman + CUSUMRandom walk + CUSUMMultivariate
S183.2%71.6%19.4%41.2%
S29.2%9.4%8.4%82.4%
S334.6%27.4%11.4%25.2%
S479.8%65.4%60.4%85.8%

Meaning. When the problem is in cash (S1), the cash-only detectors win and the multivariate one is diluted. When cash is quiet (S2) or massaged (S4), only the multivariate detector sees it. Hence the design choice to run both side by side. Honest caveat: the S1 loss (-30.4 points) is not 'slight' as the hypothesis worded it, and a plain ARIMA model beat the Kalman model on raw power here.

H2: NMC, silent cash and a warning balance sheet SUPPORTED

Result. cash flag (OCF < 0) silent FY2013-FY2018; structural flags tripped: liquidity cover < 1 first FY2015. Never tripped: EBITDA / interest < 1.5; Z''-EM < 4.35. Liquidity cover (cash and deposits ÷ short-term debt) was below 1 in FY2015, FY2017, FY2018, falling to 0.89 in 2018.

Common-sense caveat we kept

Only one of the three balance-sheet flags ever tripped, so the pre-registered archetype rule labels NMC Other, not 'Masked'. We report this rather than bend the rule. Section 7 shows why: NMC's published accounts left out billions of debt. Add hidden debt of 0.5× the reported amount or more and the same rule calls NMC Masked, years before the collapse.

H1: Jyoti, does the statistical detector warn two years early? INCONCLUSIVE

Why it could not be tested. only 0 usable ocf_to_current_liabilities value(s) in the training window (FY<= 2013); need >= 12. Requires higher-frequency pre-FY14 data (BSE quarterly FY2010-13). The simpler layers do tell the story: OCF < 0, weak interest cover and high debtor days all first trip in FY2014 (lead 3.26 years), net worth only turns negative in FY2016, and Altman Z''-EM reaches distress only in FY2018, after the event. So cash warned first, but H1 is about the statistical detector, and that needs older, higher-frequency data.

H6: Does the masking index separate crisis types? INCONCLUSIVE

In simulation the index separates 'cash drifts' (S1) from 'structure drifts' (S2) very well (AUC 0.89) and from concealment (S4) more weakly (AUC 0.64).

The cohort. 6 failed Indian firms were selected by the pre-set rule from RBI's 2017 lists, before any of their figures were read, with 5 matched controls (Videocon Industries could not be matched). Why H6 is still inconclusive: cohort of 6 failed firms collected (Other 3, Visible 3), but the masking index needs Layers 3-4, which run only with >= 12 usable periods; the most any failed firm has is 7 usable annual training values before its monitored window. Rule-level exploratory analogue in cohort_archetype_flag_order.csv.

Failed firmEvent FYArchetypeFirst cash flagFirst structural flagOrder
Amtek AutoFY2018OthernoneFY2015structural only
Bhushan Steel (Tata Steel BSL)FY2018OtherFY2013FY2015cash first
ABG ShipyardFY2018VisibleFY2013FY2014cash first
Lanco InfratechFY2018OtherFY2016FY2013structural first
Era Infra EngineeringFY2019VisibleFY2014FY2014same year
Videocon IndustriesFY2019VisibleFY2014FY2015cash first

What the cohort does show (exploratory). No firm is 'Masked' by the rule: Screener has no split of cash against short-term debt, so liquidity cover can never be checked and firms can trip at most two of three structural flags. Still, the order fits the idea behind H6: in Visible firms the cash flag came first (or in the same year), in most 'Other' firms a balance-sheet flag came first or alone. Over the years both members of a pair have data, the simple rules flagged 5 of 5 failed firms and 0 of 5 controls. With six firms this is an illustration, not proof.

On US firms, an exploratory analogue points the right way (Masked minus Visible: AUC 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.85) but the interval includes 'no effect', with only 13 Masked firms.

6. Does it work on real firms? (US EDGAR panel)

91 US firms that filed for bankruptcy and 46 matched healthy firms (same industry, similar size), monitored over the 16 quarters before each bankruptcy filing. Nothing was tuned on this data.

MethodFailed firms flaggedHealthy firms flaggedDifference (95% CI)Median warning
amber (uncorrected)62.6%54.3%+8.3 pts (-10.2 to +24.7)10.0 quarters
red (uncorrected)39.6%21.7%+17.8 pts (+2.5 to +33.1)4.5 quarters
amber (n-corrected)42.9%34.8%+8.1 pts (-10.4 to +24.5)8.0 quarters
red (n-corrected)16.5%8.7%+7.8 pts (-3.1 to +18.7)6.0 quarters
Altman Z''-EM distress91.2%52.2%+39.0 pts (+23.8 to +53.3)15.0 quarters
any Layer 2 rule92.3%45.7%+46.7 pts (+31.4 to +61.9)13.0 quarters
Finding 1: the calibration problem is real, not a simulation artefact

The uncorrected amber tier flagged 54.3% of healthy firms against a promised 10%, just as H4 predicted. The simulation-fitted correction lowered this to 34.8%, which is better but still far off: real ratios have jumps, seasonality and accounting events that the simple simulated world does not.

Finding 2: simple rules won

The pre-set rules flagged 92.3% of failed firms with 45.7% false alarms, and were the only method with a lower expected cost than Altman Z''-EM at every cost ratio tested. Most of their power comes from 'OCF < 0' alone (75.8% / 37.0%): a cash-first result, just not from the statistical layer.

Finding 3: the statistical alarms barely beat chance, and why

For the amber tiers the 95% interval of 'failed flagged minus healthy flagged' includes zero. A threshold-free check (AUC) gives 0.58 for the pre-registered cash CUSUM and 0.64 for the multivariate one, against 0.73 for simply looking at the lowest level of the cash ratio and 0.75 for the lowest Altman score. Two reasons, found after seeing the data (so they are hypotheses, not results):

  1. The model forgives slow decline. The Kalman model treats part of every change as a new 'normal level' (median firm: 26% of its variance on the moving level; a quarter of firms above 90%). A steady slide is absorbed, so the surprises stay small. The same CUSUM measured against the fixed training average scores AUC 0.65.
  2. Failing firms were weak all along. In their last training quarters, failed firms' median OCF ÷ current liabilities was already 0.35 versus 0.65 for healthy firms. A method that only asks 'is this firm worse than its own past?' cannot see a firm whose past was already bad.

The practical lesson: combine 'worse than its own past' with 'weak in absolute terms', and prefer a non-adaptive baseline for slow deterioration.

7. Robustness: do the conclusions survive changes?

These checks were added after the main results (logged as a deviation) and change one thing at a time. No verdict depends on them.

What was changedWhat happened
Re-running everything with the original settings237 of 237 firm runs identical: the pipeline is deterministic.
CUSUM allowance k ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1}; training window ±2 quarters; dropping each structural ratio; event moved a year earlierAmber false alarms stay between 43.6% and 58.6% (always far above 10%); rules keep detecting 84.8%–93.6%. The ranking of methods does not change.
Raising or lowering the threshold (× 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4)Detection and false alarms move together; no setting separates failed from healthy firms well (Figure 7A).
Each rule alone / leaving each rule outonly OCF < 0: 75.8% / 37.0%; only EBITDA / interest < 1.2: 67.0% / 30.4%; only Debtor days > 270: 2.2% / 2.2% (flagged failed / healthy). The debtor-days rule adds nothing on US firms.
Jyoti FY2017: leave missing vs fill in by interpolationCash rules unchanged (first trip FY2014), but interpolation moves Altman into distress a year early (FY2017) using an invented value. Leaving it missing was right.
Alternative event dates (one year earlier; for NMC the short-seller report of 2019-12-17)Jyoti's rule lead goes from 3.26 to 2.26 years; NMC's picture is unchanged (no rule trips, archetype Other).
NMC with hidden debt added (0×, 0.5×, 1×, 2× reported debt)Archetype becomes Masked from 0.5×; Z''-EM 2018 falls from 5.73 to -5.36. For scale: debt was later put at about US$6.6bn against US$2.1bn reported.

Common-sense catches during the project

Things that looked fine to the code but wrong to a human, and what was done about them:

  • The pre-registration hash. The config and pre-registration files were legitimately extended later (logged deviations), so their hashes no longer matched. Exact copies of the frozen versions were rebuilt from the edit history; their hashes match the recorded fingerprint, and every frozen setting is shown to be unchanged.
  • Two identical numbers in the H5 table. The detection rate of one fix equalled the false-alarm rate of another. It looked like a copy-paste bug; it is a coincidence (same count, different firms), now a permanent check.
  • A hidden source of randomness. One script seeded a model with Python's hash(), which changes every run. It never affected a result, but it would have broken reproducibility; replaced.
  • A wrong court. The NMC event was recorded as an ADGM court order; primary records show the English High Court made the 2020 order. Date unchanged, text corrected.
  • Two ratios move 'the wrong way' at bankruptcy. Failed US firms have fewer debtor days and better accruals than controls near the end. Not a sign error: big write-downs push profit below cash flow, and debtor days depend on industry. These two ratios measure earnings quality in normal times, not distress at the brink.
  • Liquidity cover is almost never available on US quarterly data because short-term debt is rarely tagged, so the structural detector usually runs without it. Recorded, not hidden.
  • An over-claim in our own text. A draft sentence said rules beat amber on false alarms 'in every variant'; the table showed one exception and one tie. The sentence is now computed from the table.
  • Earlier in the build (decision log): an identity that failed on Jyoti because of other income; interest cover blanked for healthy firms by a too-strict near-zero rule; a simulation crash from empty bootstrap pools; zero thresholds from degenerate fits, now excluded and counted; and a run that ran out of memory with too many workers.
Why the core machinery is trustworthy

If the CUSUM or threshold code were wrong, even thresholds learned from the right distribution would miss. They do not: the conformal threshold hits 4.6% for a promised 5% and 7.2% for 10%. False alarms fall as history grows, power rises with drift size, every alarm lies inside the monitored window, and the legacy scripts are reproduced exactly (numbers and pixel-identical figures).

9. Limitations

  • Two deep cases were known before the pre-registration, so they are illustrations, not tests. The cohort is the confirmatory test, but its annual data are too short for the detectors, so H6 could not be judged.
  • The cohort is small and narrow: India only (no machine-readable GCC source), events in 2017–2018, mostly steel, infrastructure and manufacturing; controls have only a few years of history on Screener's public pages.
  • Tiny samples. 6 annual points for NMC; no pre-FY14 history for Jyoti.
  • Fraud defeats ratio analysis. If debt is kept off the accounts (NMC), no ratio can see it; the hidden-debt test shows how much difference that makes.
  • Simulation realism. Gaussian AR(1) dynamics; heavy tails and training-period breaks were cut for time. The real-data results show the cost of this simplification.
  • Vendor and XBRL data. Screener proxies for Jyoti's working capital; untagged debt on EDGAR.
  • Lead times are measured from period ends, not from when the accounts were published, so real warning is shorter.
  • The multivariate detector reacts to change in any direction and can alarm on improvement.
  • The US diagnosis (Section 6) is post hoc; it should be tested on new data before being believed.

12. Viva preparation

Why not just use Altman's Z-score?
It needs no history and did well on US firms (91.2% flagged), but it also flagged 52.2% of healthy firms, and it missed NMC and warned on Jyoti only after the event. The project's point is a per-firm monitor with a known false-alarm rate, plus a way to tell visible from masked crises.
Isn't the simulation just showing what you built into it?
The simulation checks the statistics (does a promised 10% stay 10%?) under known conditions. Its main finding, over-alarming with short histories, was then confirmed on real US firms that the simulation never saw.
How do you know you didn't tune the method to fit NMC and Jyoti?
All rules and thresholds were fixed and hashed before any detector ran; the frozen settings are shown to be unchanged; deviations are logged; and NMC came out 'Other' against the story we expected, which we reported.
Your detectors barely beat chance on US data. Is the project a failure?
No: that is a finding. The calibration problem and its fixes are confirmed, the rule layer works well, and the diagnosis (adaptive models absorb slow decline; failing firms are weak for years) says how to build the next version. Reporting it honestly is the point of pre-registration.
Why is NMC not 'Masked'?
Because only one of three balance-sheet flags fired on the published numbers. With the debt that was later found, it would be Masked. Ratio analysis cannot see falsified inputs.
Why block bootstrap and not ordinary bootstrap?
Quarterly errors are correlated over time; resampling runs of consecutive values keeps that correlation.
What would you do with more time?
Get longer or quarterly histories for the cohort and Jyoti; add a non-adaptive and a level-aware detector; model heavy tails; use publication dates for lead times.
